verdict: OK to lend in Sanand auto OEM and tier-1 supply chain, but only to borrowers with contracted volumes and a clean flood-contingency record; avoid single-model, single-customer units.
title: Sanand cars & commercial vehicles (OEM): a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Sanand is an assembly town: press shops, weld and paint lines, and tier-1 feeders that turn steel, aluminium, plastics and electronics into vehicles, paid for by OEMs on negotiated schedules. **Cash sits with the OEM until the vehicle is invoiced to a dealer; the tier-1 supplier waits behind that.** Tata Motors runs the Sanand hub, building its highest-volume models — Tiago, Tigor, Nexon and Sierra [3] — and had committed to 2 lakh EVs a year at the ex-Ford Sanand plant with an additional Rs 2,000 crore of investment [2]. Treat that plant figure as a stated plan, not a verified output number.

## What has changed now
**The immediate local event is weather, not demand.** Heavy Gujarat rain and flooding halted production at Tata's Sanand plants and at several supplier units; the company told the exchange that damage assessment was under way and insurance cover existed, with recovery unclear [3]. Note the date — that report is from July 2026, so ask what has actually restarted. Demand itself is firm: Tata's Q1 FY27 net profit rose 83% to Rs 2,560 crore on volumes up 26%, with commodity inflation prompting price increases [6]. Peers echo the pattern — M&M's automotive revenue grew 25% to Rs 31,115 crore with EBIT margin at 9.5% [5], while analysts expect margin pressure from raw material and freight costs [7]. **Volume is not the risk; margin and working capital are.**

## Where the growth is
**Lend to tier-1 and tier-2 feeders with purchase orders from more than one OEM, and to logistics and warehousing serving the Sanand belt.** The data pack shows India-wide NIC 29 output up 25.2% YoY and 19.2% Apr-to-date [D], with Gujarat GST collections up 11.9% against India's 6.1% [D] — a genuine local tailwind. Bank credit to the sector is growing 27.0% against 19.2% output [D], so **part of what you will see is leverage, not demand**; when a proposal lands, check whether the loan is funding capacity or funding a receivable that is not yet due. Avoid single-model, single-OEM converters and anyone whose entire order book is one EV programme still in planning.

## How to grow safely
Structure against the receivable, not the balance sheet: **charge on receivables and inventory, monthly stock-and-book-debt statements, and a drawing power that moves with them.** Take monthly GST returns, e-way bills and OEM payment advices; quarterly, take the customer-wise sales mix. Ask every borrower for their flood and business-interruption cover and the claim status from July [3] — if cover is absent, price it in or decline. Sources say little specific about Sanand's own credit behaviour, so lean on first principles and the peer numbers above.

## Early warning signs
- **OEM schedule cuts or deferred payments** — if a tier-1's receivable days stretch beyond its own stated terms, ask for the OEM correspondence before renewing.
- **Model concentration** — if one model is over half of sales, ask what happens to the line when that model is refreshed.
- **Margin squeeze** — if gross margin falls while volumes rise, check whether price increases [6] are actually passing through.
- **Insurance gaps** — if the July flood claim is still unsettled, treat it as a cash-flow item, not a footnote.
watch: Monthly GST returns and e-way bills (monthly)
Turnover falls below the sanctioned drawing power for two months -> cut limit and ask for OEM schedule
Receivable ageing vs OEM payment advices (monthly)
Days beyond agreed terms widen -> seek OEM confirmation and reprice
Flood insurance claim status (monthly until settled)
Claim unsettled past 90 days -> treat as stressed and review facility
Single OEM or model above half of sales -> cap exposure and require diversification plan
Gross margin falls while volumes rise -> ask for price-increase evidence [6]
